title: Nsight session: microbatch power normalization and runtime overlap notes
content:
Summary

Quick notes from an ad-hoc Nsight profiling session focused on an unusual variance we saw in tail latency when microbatch size changed. The symptom: average latency stable but 99.9th latency spikes when MB=1 in CUDA-graph mode; GPU power draw and SM occupancy show transient dips during long model decode steps. Hypothesis: capture boundaries + implicit stream synchronization during graph replay cause power/SM throttling transiently, combined with microbatch size changing the KV cache pattern and memory copy overlap.

Environment / setup
- HW: NVIDIA H100s (DGX-like node) patched to driver 554.36, CUDA 12.2.
- Container: inference-runtime:prod-2027-07-30 (cuda12.2, cudnn9).
- Model: decoder-only 13B equivalent (flash-attn2 kernels, custom fused linalg), seq_len=1024 active, target_tokens=64 typical.
- Runtime flags used: --cuda-graph=enabled --persistent-kernel=false --stream-priority=true --kv-cache-policy=per-request
- Nsight command snapshot: nsys profile --stats=true --trace=cuda,nvtx --output nsight_mb1_aug10
- Complementary runs: nvprof for per-kernel metrics, and CUPTI metric collection for SM__pipe_tensor_cycles_active.avg.pct and sm__inst_executed.avg.pct

Repro steps (short)
1) Warm up with 200 inference requests (MB=4, 128 tokens).
2) Toggle microbatch sizes: MB=1,2,4 in separate runs with same total QPS.
3) Use dedicated run with CUDA graph capture enabled and then disabled for baseline.
4) Run Nsight with timeline capture for the range that includes a 99.9th spike.

Key observations from traces
- Timeline shows periodic short gaps (~400-800us) where active kernel density drops even though host threads are injecting work. These align with graph replay boundaries.
- SM efficiency (nsys metric) drops from ~84% to ~52% for a ~600us window in MB=1 captures. IPC similarly dips from 1.9 -> 1.0.
- Power telemetry from the GPU shows a corresponding dip of ~45W in the same windows; ambient GPU power normally ~260W -> dip to ~215W.
- During dips, memory copy (async memcpy H2D) is queued on the same CUDA stream as replay start, causing a small serialization we didn't expect.
- CUDA graph replay in our runtime implicitly synchronizes to ensure KV cache pointers are valid; that synchronization appears to drop the work submitted into high-priority compute streams for one scheduling quantum.
- Persistent kernels off: kernel re-launch overheads are higher, but persistent kernels introduce longer-running kernels which maintain steady power (mitigates dips) but complicate scaling across multiprocessor occupancy for small microbatches.

Representative metrics (single-run sampling window)
- MB=1, CUDA-graph ON: 99.9th latency spike window: 630us. SM active pct: 52%. Memory BW: 210 GB/s (down from 420 GB/s running outside spike). Warps active per SM: fell to ~22/64.
- MB=4, CUDA-graph ON: no significant dips; SM active pct ~79% steady.
- MB=1, CUDA-graph OFF: reduced graph-induced serialization, 99.9th spikes still appear but smaller magnitude (~320us).

Hypotheses (root causes)
1) Capture boundary synchronization: when graphs are replayed we do a small host->device coordinate step that serializes some H2D staging copies and the kernel submission path (ordering on stream 0 vs compute streams). For MB=1 the relative cost of that serialization is higher and manifests as 99.9th latency spikes.
2) Power-management hysteresis: short periods of lower sustained kernel occupancy allow the GPU to partially downclock or change power gating behavior (or NVLINK aggregator shifts), causing a larger-than-expected wall-time penalty.
3) Memory copy and copy engine contention: some H2D copies occurring on the default stream or low-priority stream are stalling compute submission when capture alignment is off.

Immediate mitigations to test
- Ensure async H2D copies use non-blocking high-priority streams and CUDA graphs capture those streams explicitly to avoid implicit syncs.
- Move critical small copies to cudaMemcpyAsync on a dedicated copy stream with cudaStreamAttachMemAsync to avoid cross-stream implicit sync.
- Experiment with persistent-kernel=true to keep a base workload that prevents power gating during microbatch=1; measure throughput/latency tradeoffs.
- Introduce a tiny pre-warm dummy kernel (nanokernel) submitted at graph-replay start to keep SMs busy while other work queues up (acts as a guard against short downclock windows).
- Adjust capture boundaries to include H2D staging where possible so replay mirrors live submission ordering.

Planned experiments (what to run next)
1) Copy stream isolation: change runtime to use dedicated copy stream + record on graph capture. Run MB=1,2,4 with/without graphs. Measure 99.9th and SM active pct. (Owner: Aisha)
2) Persistent kernel toggle grid sizing sweep: persistent-kernel on/off with varying tile sizes (block sizes) across MB sizes and check throughput vs tail-latency. (Owner: Luca)
3) Nanokernel pilot: add 50us empty compute kernel at replay start as a flag; measure whether power dip disappears. (Owner: Daniel)
4) Driver/firmware hypothesis check: schedule identical runs on a node pinned to a different driver minor patch (554.44) to rule out power governor bugs. (Owner: Priya)

Notes on measurement fidelity and pitfalls
- Nsight capture adds overhead; use short capture windows centered on the spike and compare with nvprof residuals for absolute numbers.
- CUPTI counters can be noisy at sub-ms windows; use aggregated runs (n=30) and median trimming.
- Avoid toggling system-level power modes during experiments; ensure nvidia-smi p0 is set when measuring.

Action items / decisions by next sync (Aug 18)
- Aisha: implement dedicated copy stream + graph-recording support prototype and run the MB sweep. (ETA Aug 14)
- Luca: persistent-kernel sweep and submit results with matrix of throughput vs 99.9th. (ETA Aug 16)
- Daniel: implement nanokernel hook and test amplitude/duration sensitivity. (ETA Aug 15)
- Priya: run driver-variant sanity check on two spare nodes and file INF-4821 with telemetry artifacts. (ETA Aug 13)

Loose ideas (not yet prioritized)
- Explore explicit power-management hints (if exposed) to the driver via NVML to hold clocks during short bursts. Risky for multi-tenant.
- Rework graph capture to be capture-of-graphs-per-microbatch instead of global capture; may reduce cross-request coupling.

Logs / commands used (copy/paste)
- Nsight capture: nsys profile --capture-range=cudaProfilerApi --sample=none --trace=cuda,nvtx --output ./nsight_mb1_aug10 --force-overwrite 
- CUPTI metric collection (example): cuptiActivityEnable(CUPTI_ACTIVITY_KIND_METRIC); // capture sm__pipe_tensor_cycles_active.avg.pct
- nvidia-smi monitoring: watch -n 0.5 nvidia-smi --query-gpu=power.draw,clocks.gr GHz --format=csv

Rough conclusion
There is convincing correlation between CUDA-graph replay boundaries and short-lived occupancy/power dips that disproportionately affect MB=1 runs. We have a set of low-risk mitigations (copy stream isolation, nanokernel pre-warm) and a higher-risk but potentially effective mitigation (persistent kernels). Next week’s experiments should tell us which path avoids tail-latency without regressing average throughput.

If you want raw traces: I uploaded the small Nsight nsys output to the shared bucket (see linked artifact on INF-4821) — will share direct clip once I trim PII/runtime tokens.

Notes-to-self / questions to raise in eng-sync
- Is there any internal reviewer who has prior experience fixing graph-replay-induced stalls? (cc: @Luca)
- If persistent kernels win, think about a runtime flag that enables a hybrid mode only when MB<=2.

-- Priya
